title: One membrane decides it: prokaryotic and eukaryotic cells in contact

objectives.statement: Use the nuclear-envelope test as the working criterion it is: classify the cells this lesson describes from whether a membrane encloses their DNA, sort further statements into those that follow from that answer, those it only makes possible, those that are tendencies with exceptions, and those it does not license, and state what the test does not settle, group membership being decided by ancestry.

Calculate surface area per unit volume and diffusion crossing time for a stated cell geometry, express the difference between two cells as a factor, and explain why a change in size changes those two consequences by different amounts and what each one constrains.

Explain what enclosing DNA in a nuclear envelope makes possible for the control of gene expression and what it costs, and use that trade-off together with genome size and division machinery to account for observed generation times in a gut bacterium, a human cell, and a slow-growing prokaryote.

scenes.title: Two ways to build a cell, in contact all day
scenes.contentHtml:
Two ways to build a cell, in contact all day

Scrape the inside of a colon and two populations come off on the same slide. One is the lining: tall cells joined edge to edge, each roughly 20 µm from base to tip. The other is whatever was in the tube, and it is mostly bacteria, rods and spheres about a tenth that length. Seconds earlier they were touching. A colon carries something like 3.8×10133.8\times10^{13} bacteria, the same order of magnitude as the number of cells in the whole body, and the only thing between that population and your tissue is an epithelium one cell thick.

Cell theory, scale, and emergence (PREM-BIO-001) built the crypt that supplies those lining cells and worked out why nobody could see any of this before lenses. This lesson stays at the same surface and asks a different question. Those two kinds of cell are built to different plans. What is the difference, what does each plan make easy, and what does each one cost?

One test, and everything else is downstream

Textbooks list a dozen differences between the two kinds of cell. Almost all of them are consequences or correlations. One is definitional.

Definition
id definition-two-architectureslabel Prokaryotic and eukaryotic cells

Ask a single question of any cell: is its DNA enclosed inside a membrane envelope of its own, separate from the rest of the cell's interior?

A eukaryotic cell answers yes. The envelope and the DNA it encloses are together called the cell nucleus. Your colonic lining cells are eukaryotic, as is every cell in every animal, plant, fungus, and protist.

A prokaryotic cell answers no. Its DNA sits in the same continuous interior as everything else, in a dense region called the nucleoid that is not walled off by a membrane. Bacteria are prokaryotic, and so are archaea, a second and separately named group you will meet again in this lesson.

One thing to fix before you use it. This is the working criterion, not a definition of what these groups are. It is how the two words are applied to almost every cell you will meet, it is reliable there, and it is what the rest of this lesson reasons from. It is also known to fail. One bacterium keeps its chromosomes inside membrane-bound compartments and is a bacterium anyway; scene 4 takes that case seriously, because what it shows is that membership is settled by ancestry while this test describes construction. So use the test to reason about how a cell is built. Do not use it to decide what a cell is related to, and do not expect it to answer for every cell in a body.

Everything else you will read about the two kinds of cell either follows from this answer, tends to go with it, or has nothing to do with it, and telling those three apart is most of the work here.

Two ordinary words shift meaning as you cross into this vocabulary, and both will catch you out if nobody says so.

Nucleus in everyday English means the middle, the core, the important bit. In a cell it means a specific membrane-bounded compartment with DNA inside it. A prokaryotic cell has a middle and has DNA; it has no nucleus.

Prokaryote is worse, because its etymology is an argument. It was assembled from Greek roots meaning before and kernel, so the word itself asserts that these cells came first and that the nucleus was the upgrade. Hold that claim loosely. A later scene takes it apart properly, and it is the single most common wrong idea in this topic.

What the inside of a prokaryotic cell looks like

That is a generic prokaryotic cell, opened along its length, with the nucleoid and the ribosomes sharing one continuous interior. Read it for the negative space. The DNA is a loop, usually circular, lying loose in the cytoplasm. The ribosomes, which are the machines that build protein from a transcript, are scattered through the same fluid. Nothing separates them. Compare that with a lining cell, where a transcript made in the nucleus has to be finished, checked, and moved out through the envelope before any ribosome touches it.

The other labels are there so the drawing is readable, and this lesson sources none of them beyond what it names. The cell wall outside the membrane is rigid, and that is the only one of them this lesson uses. A capsule is the layer outside the wall, a plasmid is a separate small DNA loop, pili are the short surface projections, and the flagellum is the long whip at one end. What each of those does, and how a plasmid moves between cells, is microbiology and is not established anywhere in this pack. Take the words as labels for now.

What this lesson does and does not cover

This lesson works on the contrast and its consequences: size, exchange, mixing, division rate, and what a compartment is worth. It does not open the eukaryotic interior. The nucleus is named here and left as a box with a membrane around it. Lesson 03 of this module is where the endoplasmic reticulum, Golgi, mitochondria, and the rest get their proper treatment, and lesson 04 does the membrane itself. Wait for those instead of half-learning them here.

Check
id check-recall-crypt-numbers

Before going on, recover three things from PREM-BIO-001 without looking them up.

  1. How thick is the colonic epithelium, in cells?
  2. Roughly how long does a colonic absorptive cell work at the surface before it is shed?
  3. Which side of the epithelium does the bacterial population sit on?

The epithelium is one cell thick. Much of the colonic lining turns over on a three-to-five-day timescale, with absorptive cells lasting about four to five days. The bacteria are in the lumen, the open space inside the tube, on the far side of that single layer. Hold all three: a sheet one cell thick, replacing itself every few days, with a bacterial population of order 101310^{13} pressed against it. By the end of this lesson you will be able to say why the two sides of that sheet run on such different clocks.

scenes.title: How much membrane, and how long to cross
scenes.contentHtml:
How much membrane, and how long to cross

A bacterium in the lumen is not a shrunken lining cell. Shrinking something changes two quantities that matter for staying alive, and it changes them by different amounts. Work both out and most of the differences in the rest of this lesson stop needing to be memorised.

Here is the task. A rod-shaped bacterium about 2 µm long sits against a human cell about 20 µm across. Calculate how much membrane each cell has per unit of interior, and how long a protein takes to cross each cell by diffusion alone. Then say what each result constrains.

Givens, unknowns, and what is being assumed

Quantity Value used Where it comes from
E. coli shape and size rod, about 1 µm in diameter and about 2 µm long stated for E. coli in a cell-biology textbook
Human cell size sphere 20 µm across the working figure for an animal cell, at the top of the 10 to 20 µm band
Diffusion coefficient in cytoplasm 7.7 µm² per second measured for a fluorescent protein in living E. coli

Two idealisations are doing work here and both should be said out loud. A bacterium is a rod with rounded ends and a colonic lining cell is a tall column, so treating one as a plain cylinder and the other as a sphere is a simplification. Neither cell is a smooth ball of fluid either: real interiors are crowded. These models are used because they isolate the effect of size, which is the thing being tested, and because the answers they give can be checked against measurements made another way. That check comes at the end.

The two relations, and why these two

Exchange with the outside happens across a surface. Chemistry happens in a volume. So the quantity that decides how easily a cell can supply its own interior is the surface area it has per unit of volume, written A/VA/V and carried in units of reciprocal micrometres. For a sphere the two expressions are A=4πr2A = 4\pi r^2 and V=43πr3V = \tfrac{4}{3}\pi r^3, and their ratio collapses to something worth memorising:

In words: a spherical cell's surface area per unit volume is three divided by its radius. Double the radius and you halve the ratio. Nothing about biology enters that statement; it is geometry, and it applies to any sphere.

Moving things around inside a cell, with no motor pushing them, happens by diffusion. A molecule jostled at random wanders, and the average of its squared displacement grows in proportion to elapsed time. Distance covered therefore grows only as the square root of time, and the relation rearranges to give the time needed to wander a distance xx along one direction:

Here DD is the diffusion coefficient, in square micrometres per second, and xx is a distance in micrometres, so tt comes out in seconds. The square is the whole story. Ten times the distance costs a hundred times the time.

The plan

Volumes first, because the volume ratio sets the scale of everything else. Then surfaces, then the ratio of the two. Then diffusion times at each cell's own width, holding DD fixed so that only geometry differs. Then two independent checks before believing any of it.

Step 1: volumes

For the bacterium, model a cylinder of radius r=0.5r = 0.5 µm and length L=2L = 2 µm:

For the human cell, a sphere of radius r=10r = 10 µm:

Divide: 4.2×103/1.6≈2.7×1034.2\times10^{3} / 1.6 \approx 2.7\times10^{3}. One human cell holds the volume of roughly three thousand bacteria. Between three and four orders of magnitude, then, and that is the number to carry.

Step 2: surfaces

A cylinder's surface is its curved side plus its two ends:

The sphere's surface is A=4πr2=4π(10)2≈1.3×103A = 4\pi r^{2} = 4\pi(10)^{2} \approx 1.3\times10^{3} µm².

Step 3: surface per unit volume

The second answer is exactly 3/r3/r with r=10r = 10 µm, which is a small confirmation that the arithmetic held. Dividing one by the other: 5.0/0.30≈175.0 / 0.30 \approx 17. Every cubic micrometre of bacterial interior is served by about seventeen times as much membrane as every cubic micrometre of human-cell interior.

That curve is worth pausing on. Between 0.25 and 1 µm of radius it falls off a cliff; past about 5 µm it is nearly flat. A bacterium that grows half a micrometre wider pays a real price in membrane per unit of interior. A human cell that grows half a micrometre wider barely notices. The same physical relation is a hard constraint at one size and a non-issue at the other.

Step 4: how long a protein takes to cross

Use t=x2/2Dt = x^{2}/2D with D=7.7D = 7.7 µm² per second, and take xx as the distance across each cell.

Ten times the distance, a hundred times the time. In a bacterium, a newly made protein reaches the far end in about a quarter of a second, so nothing inside is ever far from anything else. In a cell 20 µm across, the same journey by diffusion alone takes half a minute, and half a minute is a long time if what is arriving is a signal.

Step 5: check it two ways before believing it

The first check is a measurement nobody made for this purpose. Our modelled bacterium came out at 1.6 µm³, which is 1.6 femtolitres. A study that measured E. coli volume across 22 growth conditions found single-cell volumes from 1.5 to 4.4 femtolitres. The model lands at the bottom of the measured range, which is where a cylinder built from the smaller quoted dimensions should land. It is not proof that the model is right; it is evidence that it is not wildly wrong.

The second check is on the volume ratio. A textbook statement, arrived at independently of this arithmetic, is that eukaryotic cells are frequently at least a thousandfold greater in volume than prokaryotic cells. Our figure of roughly three thousand sits comfortably above that floor.

Both checks pass, so the two headline numbers stand: a factor of about 17 in membrane per unit volume, and a factor of 100 in diffusion time.

The assumptions you would attack first

The diffusion coefficient was measured inside E. coli and then applied to both cells. That was deliberate: holding DD fixed isolates geometry, which is what the comparison is testing.

It is worth seeing how much the answer moves when the idealisation is dropped. Measured in the cytoplasm of cultured mammalian cells, the same fluorescent protein diffuses at about 26 µm² per second, more than three times faster than in E. coli. Redo the second calculation with that value and the crossing time falls from 26 s to about 7.7 s. The gap between the two cells narrows from a factor of 100 to a factor of about 30, and the conclusion survives: crossing the larger cell is one to two orders of magnitude slower whichever value you use. A comparison that changes by a factor of three when a questionable assumption is corrected, while its conclusion holds, is a comparison worth keeping.

A second limit worth naming is that a real cell does not rely on diffusion alone. Directed transport, cytoskeletal tracks, and bulk flow all exist, and lesson 07 is where they arrive. What the calculation establishes is what unaided diffusion can and cannot deliver, which is the baseline everything else has to beat.

Before moving on, answer this in your own words: why does holding the diffusion coefficient fixed strengthen the comparison rather than weaken it? If your answer mentions accuracy, try again; the question is about what the calculation is for.

What the two numbers constrain

The surface ratio constrains supply. A bacterium can take up what it needs across a generous surface and its metabolism can run fast, which is part of why it can rebuild itself in the time a human cell takes to do very much less. The diffusion result constrains coordination. A cell 2 µm long can leave its parts loose in one compartment and rely on everything finding everything else. A cell 20 µm across cannot, and the next scene is about what it does instead.

scenes.title: A room of its own, and the rent it charges
scenes.contentHtml:
A room of its own, and the rent it charges

Twenty-six seconds is the number scene 2 left on the table. That is how long a protein needs to cross a 20 µm cell if nothing is pushing it. A bacterium never faces that problem, because a quarter of a second is not a delay anybody has to plan around. So the eukaryotic cell is stuck with distances that diffusion handles badly, and it has an internal membrane where the bacterium has none. What is that membrane worth?

What the envelope buys

Start with what happens when a gene is read. DNA is transcribed into RNA, and RNA is translated by ribosomes into protein. Where those two steps happen relative to each other is decided entirely by the criterion from scene 1.

In a bacterium the two steps share one space. A ribosome can bind a transcript that RNA polymerase is still making and begin translating the front of it while the back is still being written. Transcription and translation run coupled, and that arrangement is characteristic of prokaryotic gene expression. Nothing stands between the polymerase and the ribosome, because nothing can.

In a eukaryotic cell a membrane stands between them, for the genes in the nucleus. Transcription of a nuclear gene happens inside the envelope; translation happens outside it. A transcript therefore cannot be read at the moment it is made. It has to be finished, chemically modified at both ends, have its non-coding stretches removed, pass quality control, and be exported through the envelope. Only then does a ribosome see it.

The qualification is not pedantry. A eukaryotic cell also carries DNA in its mitochondria, outside the nucleus, and those genes are transcribed and translated in the same compartment as each other. The separation this scene is about is a property of the nuclear genome, not of every gene a eukaryotic cell owns. Lesson 03 of this module opens that compartment.

That sequence is an opportunity, and it is the real answer to what the envelope buys. Every one of those steps is a place where the cell can decide something: whether this transcript is exported at all, which version of it is assembled, whether it is held back or destroyed. A compartment converts a one-step process into a staged one, and each stage is a control point. Compartmentalisation, in this lesson's sense, means exactly that: separating incompatible or sequential activities into different membrane-bounded spaces so that each can be run and regulated on its own terms.

Be exact about the word opportunity, because it is a tier of its own and the next scene will make you sort by it. The envelope directly causes one thing: a nuclear transcript cannot be read where it was made, so it has to cross first. Everything in the list after that — the modifications, the removal of non-coding stretches, the quality check, the choice of whether to export — is made possible by that separation and is not caused by it. A membrane inspects nothing. Each of those steps needs its own machinery, which the cell also has to build and run, and a cell could in principle have the compartment and do very little with it. So there are two different strengths of claim here, and running them together is the commonest way this topic goes wrong: the separation follows from the criterion, and the regulation is what the separation opens up.

One further qualification belongs beside that claim, not after it. Coupling in prokaryotes is not uniform. How tightly transcription and translation run together varies between bacterial species and with growth conditions, so "bacteria always couple, eukaryotes never do" overstates a real difference into a law. The structural statement is the safe one: a eukaryotic cell has a compartment boundary available to regulate at, and a prokaryotic cell does not.

What it costs

Every gate is also a delay and a piece of machinery. A eukaryotic cell pays for its regulatory layer in transport: transcripts out, proteins in, each through pores, each requiring the apparatus that recognises what is allowed through. A bacterium responding to a change in its surroundings can have new protein appearing while the gene is still being read. A eukaryotic cell cannot match that, and for a cell whose job is to hold a barrier for four days and then be replaced, it does not need to.

The cost shows up hardest at division, and the reason is arithmetic about copying.

Prokaryotic cell Eukaryotic human cell
DNA to copy 4.6 million base pairs in E. coli, and 0.6 to 5 million across bacteria generally about 3.05 billion base pairs
Arrangement usually a single circular molecule in the nucleoid linear molecules across 23 distinct chromosomes
Extra work at division none of the following condense chromosomes, build a spindle, take the envelope apart, rebuild it
Time for one cycle 17 to 18 minutes in rich broth at 37 °C, and 51 to 54 minutes in a minimal medium about 24 hours for human cells in culture

The DNA row alone is a factor of order a thousand. A human cell has to duplicate roughly a thousand times as much sequence, spread over more than twenty separate molecules that then have to be sorted so each daughter receives a full set. Sorting is the part that needs mitosis, and mitosis needs the envelope taken down and put back. Of the roughly 24 hours a cultured human cell spends on one cycle, mitosis and the division itself occupy about an hour; the other 95% is spent getting ready.

Check
id check-generations-in-a-renewal

PREM-BIO-001 established that much of the colonic lining is replaced on a three-to-five-day timescale, with absorptive cells lasting about four to five days.

Take four days as the renewal interval and 20 minutes as a bacterial doubling time. How many bacterial generations fit inside one renewal of the lining? Then say why the number you get is an upper bound rather than an estimate of what happens in a colon.

Four days is 96 hours, which is 5760 minutes, and 5760 divided by 20 is 288 generations. In the time the lining rebuilds itself once, a bacterium at laboratory speed could run through nearly three hundred.

The number is an upper bound, and the measurements say so themselves. Seventeen to eighteen minutes is what E. coli manages in rich broth at 37 °C; the same organism in a defined minimal medium takes 51 to 54 minutes, three times longer, and neither flask is a colon. Growth in the gut is limited by what is available, by competition with everything else living there, and by being carried along and out. Treating a maximum as a measurement is the error to avoid. What survives the caveat is the direction and the size of the gap: the two sides of that epithelium run on clocks that differ by orders of magnitude, whatever the exact numbers.

What the asymmetry forces

A sheet of cells cannot win a race against a population that divides that much faster. Out-multiplying the lumen is not available, and it never was. So the epithelium does something else: it excludes. It keeps a continuous barrier, it renews itself before individual cells wear out, and it holds the bacteria on the far side instead of competing with them.

That is where the rest of this module goes. Lesson 03 opens the eukaryotic interior and shows what all those compartments are actually doing. Lesson 04 asks what the barrier is made of. Lesson 07 asks what physically joins one lining cell to the next, and lesson 08 returns to the cell cycle with the machinery to explain the 24 hours properly.

scenes.title: Older, simpler, lesser: three words that do not follow
scenes.contentHtml:
Older, simpler, lesser: three words that do not follow

Commit to an answer before reading on. True or false, and why?

  1. Prokaryotic cells are an earlier form that eukaryotic cells improved on.
  2. Prokaryotic cells have no internal compartments.
  3. If a cell is large, it is eukaryotic.

Most people who meet this topic answer true, true, true. The wording of the vocabulary encourages it, and so does the order textbooks present things in. Each answer is wrong, and the third is wrong in a way that reveals what the other two are doing.

The model to take apart

Here is the idea in its most reasonable form, stated as someone holding it would state it. Life began simple. Early cells had no internal structure, just DNA and enzymes loose in a bag. Later, a compartment appeared around the DNA, and that innovation made everything else possible: bigger cells, more genes, specialisation, multicellularity. Prokaryotes are what remains of the first stage; eukaryotes are the second stage. The prefix says so.

Nothing about that story is stupid. It has a beginning, a middle, and a mechanism, and parts of it are even true. What it gets wrong is the shape of the claim: it converts a structural description into a ranking, and a ranking implies a ladder that the evidence does not support.

Three things the ranking cannot account for

A group defined by an absence need not be a branch. Prokaryote covers two collections of organisms, bacteria and archaea. In 1990 Woese, Kandler and Wheelis argued from molecular sequence data that the living world divides primarily into three domains, Bacteria, Archaea and Eucarya, and that neither the five-kingdom scheme nor the prokaryote–eukaryote dichotomy captures that primary division. A domain in this sense is a rank in classification, sitting above kingdom; it is a different use of the word from the domain of a function in Functions and graphs (PREM-QNT-007), and the two senses share nothing but the spelling. Work since has gone further: phylogenomic analyses place eukaryotes as emerging from within the Archaea, with the Asgard archaea as their closest prokaryotic relatives. Read that carefully. If eukaryotes arose from inside one of the two groups that "prokaryote" collects, then "prokaryote" is not a limb of the tree with eukaryotes on a different limb. It is a description of cells that lack a particular feature, and organisms lacking a feature can sit anywhere.

Prokaryotic cells build compartments. Bacteria are routinely described as having organelles. Some are membrane-bound: anammoxosomes, magnetosomes, chromatophores, chlorosomes. Others are built from protein rather than lipid, and the best studied is the carboxysome, which encloses the enzymes of carbon fixation behind a selectively permeable protein shell. Concentrating a reaction, keeping a toxic intermediate away from the rest of the cell, controlling what diffuses in and out: prokaryotes do all of it. The thing they lack is specifically an envelope around the chromosome.

Size is a tendency with a spectacular exception. Candidatus Thiomargarita magnifica reaches about 2 cm in length and 50 µm across. Two centimetres is roughly ten thousand times the length of the rod modelled in scene 2, and longer than a great many animals. Read the second half of that description too: in this organism, one or more chromosomes sit inside membrane-bound compartments called pepins.

That last fact should bother you, and it is supposed to. A criterion stated as a bright line has met an organism that sits on the line, which is what happens to structural criteria when biology is sampled widely enough. What biologists did in response is the instructive part. They did not reclassify it as a eukaryote. It is a bacterium because of what its genome and ribosomal RNA say about its ancestry, and ancestry is settled by sequence comparison rather than by counting membranes. The architecture criterion from scene 1 describes how a cell is built. It was never the thing that decides who is related to whom, and treating a description of construction as a verdict on lineage is the root error inside all three false statements above.

What the criterion actually licenses

Use it as a sorting rule. When you meet a claim about the two cell types, ask which tier it belongs to.

  • Does it follow from where the DNA sits? Then it is safe.
  • Is it something the arrangement makes possible, needing machinery of its own? Then it holds where somebody has checked that the machinery is there. Transcript quality control is the example from the last scene: the envelope opens the possibility and does not do the work.
  • Is it a tendency? Then it holds until you meet the exception, and you have now met two.
  • Is it about rank, age, or worth? Then the criterion has nothing to say, and neither should you.

And one thing sits outside the tiers altogether, which is what group an organism belongs to. That is ancestry, and the giant bacterium above is the proof: the test answers enclosed for it and it is a bacterium anyway.

Misconception
id misconception-prokaryote-means-primitive

The wrong model. Prokaryotic cells are the primitive first draft; the nucleus is the upgrade that produced everything since.

What it cannot explain. Eukaryotes arise from within the Archaea, so the two groups the term collects are not a single lineage that eukaryotes departed from. Bacteria build compartments, including membrane-bound organelles and protein-shelled ones. A bacterium exists that is 2 cm long with chromosomes in membrane-bound compartments.

The model that survives. The prokaryote–eukaryote distinction describes one architectural feature: whether a membrane envelope encloses the DNA. It predicts where transcription and translation can happen. It correlates loosely with cell size and division rate. It says nothing about age, complexity, sophistication, or evolutionary rank, and it is not how relatedness is established.

Check
id check-classify-the-new-organism

A constructed case, written for this exercise rather than taken from a real report. A microbe recovered from deep-sea sediment is described as follows.

  • Cells about 8 µm across.
  • A single circular chromosome lying free in the cytoplasm.
  • An internal compartment with a protein shell, concentrating one enzyme.
  • A doubling time of about 30 hours.

Classify it, then say which of the four descriptions you used and why the other three were set aside.

It is prokaryotic, and only the second description was needed: the chromosome lies free in the cytoplasm, so no membrane envelope encloses it.

The other three are distractors of three different kinds. The 8 µm width is a tendency running the wrong way, and tendencies do not classify; the centimetre-long bacterium already showed that a large prokaryotic cell is possible. The protein-shelled compartment is not a nucleus and never was, so it is irrelevant to a criterion about the DNA specifically; carboxysomes are exactly this. The 30-hour doubling time is another tendency running the wrong way, and the next scene is built around a real organism that behaves the same way. If you found yourself weighing the four facts against each other and taking a majority verdict, that is the habit to break. One of them is the one the criterion reads and three of them are noise. Note the careful wording: the criterion reads the DNA's location, and that is what makes it the relevant fact here. It is not that the location defines what the organism is, which is the thing the giant bacterium settled.

scenes.title: Four problems, and less help each time
scenes.contentHtml:
Four problems, and less help each time

Work each one before opening its feedback. The first hands you the relations, the second hands you a rule to apply, the third and fourth hand you nothing.

First pass: the relations are supplied

You need two things from scene 2. For a sphere of radius rr, surface area per unit volume is A/V=3/rA/V = 3/r. For a molecule wandering by diffusion with coefficient DD, the time to cover a distance xx is t=x2/2Dt = x^{2}/2D. Take D=7.7D = 7.7 µm² per second throughout.

Check
id check-coccus-arithmetic

A spherical bacterium is 1 µm across. A colonic lining cell is modelled as a sphere 20 µm across.

  1. What is A/VA/V for each, in reciprocal micrometres?
  2. By what factor do they differ?
  3. How long does a protein take to cross each cell by diffusion?
  4. By what factor do those two times differ, and why is that factor not the same as the one in question 2?

Feedback after your attempt

The spherical bacterium has r=0.5r = 0.5 µm, so A/V=3/0.5=6A/V = 3/0.5 = 6 µm⁻¹. The lining cell has r=10r = 10 µm, so A/V=3/10=0.3A/V = 3/10 = 0.3 µm⁻¹. They differ by a factor of 20.

Crossing times: t=12/(2×7.7)≈0.065t = 1^{2}/(2 \times 7.7) \approx 0.065 s for the bacterium and t=202/(2×7.7)≈26t = 20^{2}/(2 \times 7.7) \approx 26 s for the lining cell. Those differ by a factor of 400.

Question 4 is the one worth getting right. Both cells differ by a factor of 20 in size, but the two consequences scale differently: surface per unit volume goes as 1/r1/r, so it changes by 20, while diffusion time goes as x2x^{2}, so it changes by 202=40020^{2} = 400. Growing a cell hurts its mixing far more than it hurts its supply. If you got 400 for both, or 20 for both, go back to the two relations and read the exponents.

Second pass: a rule to apply

Every claim below is true of some cells. Sort each into one of three boxes: follows from the criterion, tendency with exceptions, or not licensed by the criterion at all. Give one line of reason each.

Check
id check-sort-the-claims
  1. A ribosome can begin translating a transcript that is still being made.
  2. The cell is less than 10 µm across.
  3. The cell's design came first in evolutionary history.
  4. Transcripts are modified and checked before any ribosome reads them.
  5. The cell divides in under an hour.
  6. The cell has no internal compartments of any kind.
  7. The cell is less sophisticated than the other type.

Feedback after your attempt

Follows from the criterion: items 1 and 4. Both are statements about where transcription and translation sit relative to each other, which is decided entirely by whether a membrane separates the DNA from the ribosomes. Item 1 describes prokaryotic cells and item 4 eukaryotic ones.

Tendency with exceptions: items 2 and 5. Prokaryotic cells are usually small and usually fast, and you have already met a bacterium 2 cm long, with a slow one arriving in the next scene.

Not licensed at all: items 3, 6 and 7. Item 3 asks about evolutionary history, which is settled by sequence comparison, not by architecture, and eukaryotes emerge from within the Archaea rather than after prokaryotes as a whole. Item 6 is simply false: bacteria build carboxysomes, magnetosomes and other organelles. Item 7 is not a biological claim; it is a ranking with no measurement behind it.

Item 6 is the one people misfile. It feels like it should follow, because the criterion is about a compartment. It does not follow, because the criterion is about one compartment, around one thing.

Third pass: no support

Check
id check-engineer-a-large-bacterium

Someone proposes engineering a bacterium to be 20 µm across while leaving its internal organisation unchanged: one nucleoid, ribosomes loose in the cytoplasm, no internal compartments.

Using only quantities this lesson has established, name the two problems this creates and say how large each one is. Then say whether either is fatal, and give the evidence for your answer.

Feedback after your attempt

Both problems are the ones from the first pass, and both get worse together.

Surface per unit volume falls from about 6 µm⁻¹ at 1 µm across to about 0.3 µm⁻¹ at 20 µm across, a factor of 20. Everything the cell takes in or throws out crosses its surface, and each unit of interior now has a twentieth of the membrane serving it.

Diffusion time across the cell rises from about 0.065 s to about 26 s, a factor of 400. With one nucleoid and no internal organisation, a protein made at one end takes half a minute to reach the other, and a signal that needs a response has to wait that long before anything can happen.

Neither is fatal, and the evidence is that a 2 cm bacterium exists. What that organism does not do is keep the internal organisation unchanged, which is the condition the proposal insists on. It carries chromosomes inside membrane-bound compartments and has enormous numbers of genome copies, so a transcript never has to travel the full length of the cell. Take the compartments away and the arithmetic above is what remains. The general form of the answer is the useful one: size is survivable, and what it costs is a demand for internal organisation that scales with it.

Fourth pass: explain it to somebody

Check
id check-explain-to-a-friend

A friend studying for the same exam says: "So the difference is that prokaryotes are simpler, and everything else follows from that."

Write three sentences that repair the claim without using the words simple, primitive, advanced, or higher. Your first sentence must state what the actual criterion is.

Feedback after your attempt

Compare yours with this. "The difference is whether a membrane envelope encloses the cell's DNA; eukaryotic cells have one and prokaryotic cells do not. That envelope decides where transcription and translation happen, so a eukaryotic cell can process and check a transcript before any ribosome reads it, while a bacterial ribosome can start on a transcript that is still being made. Everything else you have heard about the two types, including size and division rate, is a tendency with real exceptions, and none of it ranks one type above the other."

Your version does not need to match that. It needs to open with the criterion, name at least one consequence that genuinely follows from it, and mark the rest as tendency. If your first sentence was about size, division rate, or organelles in general, the repair has not taken hold yet.

Where to go next

  • All four passes right: continue to the culture-room problem in the next scene.
  • Trouble in the first pass: the fault is almost always the exponent. Write both relations on one line, A/V=3/rA/V = 3/r and t=x2/2Dt = x^{2}/2D, and say aloud which one squares.
  • Trouble in the second pass: run the sorting rule in writing, in order. Ask "does this depend on where the DNA sits?" before anything else, and only then ask whether the claim is a tendency.
  • Trouble in the third or fourth pass: those need the first two working, so go back instead of forward.

Recovery route

If the algebra in scene 2 was the sticking point and not the biology, the shortest repair is Units and dimensional analysis (PREM-QNT-002). Everything here is one multiplication or one division, and the errors are nearly always in carrying µm, µm² and µm³ through a quotient.

If comparing 101310^{13} with 10−610^{-6} still feels unfamiliar, return to Powers, roots, and scale (PREM-QNT-005). This lesson compares quantities by order of magnitude constantly and does not re-teach it.

If the crypt is not yet a clear picture, go back to Cell theory, scale, and emergence (PREM-BIO-001) before continuing. Every scene here assumes a tube of epithelium one cell thick, renewing itself every few days, with the lumen on one side.

If the word prokaryote keeps pulling you back toward primitive, try a mechanical substitution for a week. Every time you read or write it, say "cell with no envelope around its DNA" in your head. The phrase is clumsy and that is the point: it carries only what the term is entitled to carry.

If you are still unsure after another reading, ask your course text or instructor before pressing on. Lesson 03 assumes the compartmentalisation argument from scene 3 and builds directly on it.

scenes.title: Why one culture reads out overnight and another takes six weeks
scenes.contentHtml:
Why one culture reads out overnight and another takes six weeks

Three specimens reach a hospital microbiology bench on a Monday morning. One is a stool sample, plated to look for enteric bacteria. One is sputum from a patient with a chronic cough and weight loss, set up to look for Mycobacterium tuberculosis. One is a tissue biopsy going to a research laboratory to be grown as a primary human cell culture.

Before reading further, predict the order in which those three will give an answer, and by roughly how much they will differ. Then read on, because one of the three will not do what the tendency predicts.

The estimate you can do from this lesson

A colony on an agar plate is visible to the naked eye when it holds a large number of cells. Take 10⁸ cells as the threshold; that figure is an assumption of this exercise rather than a measured constant, and the answer will be checked against something independent in a moment.

Starting from one cell, reaching 10⁸ takes nn doublings where 2n=1082^{n} = 10^{8}, so n=8/log10⁡2≈27n = 8/\log_{10}2 \approx 27. Twenty-seven doublings, whatever the organism. Only the length of a doubling differs.

Check
id check-time-to-a-visible-colony

Work out how long 27 doublings takes for each of these, and give the answer in the unit a laboratory would use.

  1. E. coli in rich broth at 37 °C, doubling in about 18 minutes.
  2. E. coli in a defined minimal medium at 37 °C, doubling in about 52 minutes.
  3. M. tuberculosis on enriched media, doubling in about 24 hours.

Twenty-seven doublings at 18 minutes is 486 minutes, a little over eight hours: set the plate up in the afternoon and read it in the morning. At 52 minutes it is 1404 minutes, close to a full day. At 24 hours it is 648 hours, which is 27 days, or near enough four weeks.

Now the independent check. Published figures for M. tuberculosis say identifiable colonies may not appear for four to six weeks on solid media inoculated with clinical material, and the 2014 study cited here reports a primary culture obtained in two to four weeks on average. Our estimate of about four weeks lands inside that band, from an assumed colony size and a published doubling time, with nothing fitted to the answer. The estimate is doing real work instead of being decorated with a number.

The part that breaks the tendency

M. tuberculosis is a prokaryotic cell. Its DNA lies in the cytoplasm with no envelope around it, exactly as in the cutaway figure in scene 1. Its doubling time on enriched media is 18 to 24 hours.

A cultured human cell divides about once every 24 hours, and an intestinal stem cell in a crypt divides about once a day.

Those two numbers are the same. A bacterium and a human cell, the two architectures this lesson has spent five scenes contrasting, dividing at the same rate. If you predicted at the top of this scene that the bacterial culture would beat the human one, you were applying the tendency tier as though it were the criterion tier, which is the exact error scene 4 was built to prevent.

Nothing about the classification changes. M. tuberculosis is not less prokaryotic for being slow, and the sputum culture is not evidence against anything the criterion claims. What the case shows is where in the scene 4 diagram the statement "prokaryotes divide fast" belongs: on the tendency branch, with counterexamples, alongside "prokaryotes are small".

Why a mycobacterium is slow is a real question and this lesson does not answer it; the cause lies in its unusual cell envelope and its metabolism rather than in the presence or absence of a nucleus. What matters here is that the lesson's model tells you exactly how surprised to be, which is not very.

What the delay costs a patient

Turnaround time is not an administrative detail. A stool culture answering overnight means a decision the next day. A mycobacterial culture answering in four to six weeks, with drug-susceptibility testing needing another two to four weeks after that, means treatment decisions get made long before the culture confirms them. That gap is why tuberculosis diagnosis now leads with molecular methods that do not wait for growth, while culture and phenotypic susceptibility testing stay slow and stay necessary. It is also why a negative mycobacterial culture at two weeks has to be read as weak evidence rather than as a result. How weak depends on the specimen, how many organisms were in it, and which system the laboratory used, and none of those are things this lesson can settle for you. The timings above come from one 2014 study and describe culture, not the diagnosis a patient receives today.

This is a teaching example and not clinical guidance, and it prescribes nothing. What it illustrates is that a doubling time measured in a flask propagates all the way to how a clinic is run.

Check
id check-transfer-new-organism-turnaround

A laboratory reports that a newly characterised gut organism forms visible colonies in about three days at 37 °C.

  1. Estimate its doubling time, using the same 27-doubling assumption.
  2. Does that estimate tell you whether the organism is prokaryotic or eukaryotic? Say what would.
  3. Name one thing that could make your estimate wrong even if the doubling time is correct.

Three days is 72 hours; 72 divided by 27 is about 2.7 hours per doubling. That places it between E. coli and M. tuberculosis, and it tells you nothing whatever about the cell's architecture. Deciding that requires looking at where the DNA sits, which in practice means microscopy with a stain that shows a nucleus, or sequence data placing the organism among relatives whose cell type is known.

For the third question, the assumption most likely to be wrong is the colony threshold of 10⁸ cells, which varies with the organism and the medium. A colony visible at 10⁷ cells needs only about 23 doublings, which spreads the same 72 hours over fewer of them and lengthens the estimated doubling time to about 3.1 hours. A lag phase before growth begins pushes the estimate the other way, because less of the 72 hours was spent doubling at all. Both are reasons this is an estimate with an error bar you cannot yet put a number on, which is the honest description of most first estimates.

scenes.title: Clinical wrap-up: the drug that can tell your cells from theirs
scenes.contentHtml:
Clinical wrap-up: the drug that can tell your cells from theirs

Someone swallows a tablet for a chest infection. Over the next few hours it reaches essentially every tissue, including the colon, where it meets a bacterial population of about 10¹¹ organisms per millilitre of contents lying against an epithelium one cell thick. The tablet kills bacteria. It does not kill the patient.

That is a strange thing for a small molecule to manage, and this lesson's model explains part of it, misses part of it, and predicts the most important side effect. Work through it in that order.

Callout

A teaching example, not medical advice. Nothing here is a recommendation about any drug, dose, patient, or decision, and no drug is named as a treatment for anything. The point is to show the lesson's model doing work on a real clinical question.

Part the model explains

Both cell types build protein on ribosomes. The ribosomes are not the same. A bacterial ribosome and a eukaryotic cytoplasmic ribosome differ enough in sequence and structure that a molecule can bind one and not the other, and the difference that decides it is sometimes a single nucleotide or a single amino acid.

That difference is enough for whole drug classes. Eukaryotic cytoplasmic ribosomes are insensitive to macrolides, lincosamides, streptomycin and 2-deoxystreptamines, while bacterial ribosomes are sensitive to them. A drug of that kind, arriving in a tissue where a bacterium sits next to a human cell, shuts down protein synthesis in one and leaves the other running.

Now place that fact in the right tier of the diagram from scene 4. The ribosome difference does not follow from the nuclear envelope. Nothing about a membrane around DNA determines the sequence of a ribosomal RNA. It is a difference between two lineages that also happen to differ in architecture, which puts it on the correlate branch. Getting this right matters, because a learner who files it under "follows from the criterion" will make a prediction the next section shows to be wrong.

Part the model misses

Look inside a human cell, at the mitochondria. Their ribosomes retain bacterial-like features, enough that they are susceptible to drugs the cell's cytoplasmic ribosomes shrug off. The proposal in the literature is that the toxicity of ribosome-targeting drugs in patients is most likely a consequence of that susceptibility, and the ototoxicity and nephrotoxicity that limit aminoglycoside use are the standing example.

So the two-architecture picture has a seam running through the inside of your own cells. A eukaryotic cell contains a compartment whose protein-synthesis machinery answers to the other side of the divide. Why that should be is lesson 03's subject and it is worth waiting for; the endosymbiotic origin of mitochondria is one of the better stories in cell biology and it deserves more than a sentence here. What this scene needs is only the consequence: a criterion about where the DNA sits does not carry all the way down to every machine in the cell, and a clinical prediction built on assuming it does will be too optimistic.

What the model predicts, and the crypt confirms

Return to the colon. The drug is selective between cell architectures. It is not selective between one bacterium and another.

Everything in the lumen that is susceptible is hit. The resident population is not a bystander in that tissue; it occupies the space and the resources that would otherwise be available to something else, and removing it removes that occupancy. Perturbing the gut microbiota with antibiotics is what allows Clostridioides difficile spores to germinate into vegetative cells, colonise, and produce toxins. Those toxins, TcdA and TcdB, inactivate proteins of the Rho family, which alters cell integrity and shape, breaks the tight junctions between neighbouring cells, and increases the permeability of the intestinal epithelial layer. The clinical range runs from mild diarrhoea to pseudomembranous colitis and toxic megacolon.

Read that last paragraph against scene 3. A sheet of cells one thick, dividing about once a day, cannot out-multiply a population that at laboratory speed doubles in under twenty minutes. Its entire strategy is exclusion: stay continuous, replace worn cells before they fail, and keep the lumen on the lumen side. That strategy has a hidden dependency, which is that the population on the far side stays roughly the same population. A drug chosen for its ability to distinguish two cell architectures does its most serious damage precisely at the surface where those two architectures meet.

Check
id check-predict-the-selectivity

Answer from the model rather than from memory.

  1. A new drug binds a structure present in bacterial cells and absent from human cells. Does that guarantee it is safe for a patient? Name the specific thing this lesson says to check.
  2. A colleague argues that because the drug cannot enter the nucleus, it cannot harm a human cell. Say what is wrong with the argument.
  3. Predict one consequence of giving that drug to someone whose colonic epithelium is already damaged, and say which part of this lesson supports the prediction.

For the first question: no. Check the mitochondria. A structure absent from the eukaryotic cytoplasm may still be present, in a bacterial-like form, inside a compartment of the same cell, and ribosome-targeting drugs are the documented case.

For the second, the argument assumes that "eukaryotic cell" means "everything important happens behind the nuclear envelope". Most of what a drug can interfere with is outside the nucleus: ribosomes, membranes, metabolism, and the mitochondrial compartment. The criterion locates the DNA and nothing else.

For the third, a reasonable prediction is that removing the resident population from the lumen makes an already-compromised barrier worse instead of better, because the epithelium's exclusion strategy depends on the community on the far side staying stable. The support is the antibiotic-perturbation route to C. difficile colonisation and the toxin damage to junctions and permeability described above. This is a prediction about mechanism, not a claim about how often it happens in any particular group of patients, and nothing here should be read as advice about a real decision.

Where this leaves you, and what comes back later

Six scenes ago the question was what separates a bacterium in the lumen from the cell it is touching. The answer turned out to be one structural fact with a short list of genuine consequences and a long list of things people wrongly attach to it.

Carry four things forward.

The criterion: whether a membrane envelope encloses the DNA, and nothing else.

The arithmetic: surface per unit volume goes as 1/r1/r and diffusion time goes as x2x^{2}, so a cell twenty times larger has a twentieth of the membrane per unit interior and takes four hundred times as long to mix.

The trade: a compartment buys staged control and charges transport and time.

The discipline: sort every claim about the two cell types into follows, tends to, or does not follow, before you use it.

Lesson 03 opens the eukaryotic interior that this lesson deliberately left shut, and it will ask you to reuse the diffusion argument to explain why a cell 20 µm across needs compartments at all. Lesson 08 returns to the 24-hour cell cycle with the machinery to explain it. Lesson 10 comes back to the crypt when division stops being controlled. When any of those arrives, recover the surface-to-volume relation and the crossing-time relation from memory first, before rereading; that retrieval is worth more than the reread.

Accessibility and alternatives

Every task in this lesson can be answered in prose, a list, or a table, whichever suits you, and typed, dictated, or entered through assistive technology. All arithmetic is one or two steps and can be done on paper, in your head, or with a calculator; answers are ranges, and an estimate anywhere inside a stated range is correct.

The three visuals each carry a text equivalent that contains everything they are used for. The labelled prokaryotic cell has a long description that names every structure, states where each sits relative to the others, and gives the teaching point, which is that no membrane runs between the DNA and the ribosomes. The surface-to-volume chart has a long description listing the ratio at eleven radii and both marked positions, so the curve's shape and the two comparisons are available as numbers. The criterion diagram is a list of nodes and labelled links, and its long description states the three tiers and which statements sit in each. No task depends on seeing any of them, and none of the three encodes information by colour alone.

Nothing here depends on position on a page, dragging, sound, motion, or speed. No task asks about your own body, health, medication, infections, or test results, and no activity involves handling, culturing, or being exposed to any organism.

assessment.title: Prokaryotic and eukaryotic cells: classification, size constraints, and the cost of a compartment

items.prompt: An organism recovered from a hot spring is described in a report as follows: cells about 3 micrometres across; a single circular chromosome lying in the cytoplasm with no membrane around it; internal compartments with protein shells that concentrate one enzyme; a generation time of about 40 hours. Which classification does the architectural criterion support, and on what?

options.text: Prokaryotic, because the chromosome lies in the cytoplasm with no membrane enclosing it.
Eukaryotic, because the cell has internal compartments.
Eukaryotic, because a 40-hour generation time is far too slow for a prokaryotic cell.
It cannot be decided, because the four descriptions point in different directions.

answer.summary: Prokaryotic, decided by the location of the chromosome alone.
answer.reasoning: The criterion asks one question: is the DNA enclosed by a membrane envelope of its own? Here it is not, so the criterion supports prokaryotic, which is what the prompt asked. Note what that does and does not mean. The criterion describes how the cell is built. It is not what decides which group the organism belongs to, and the lesson supplies the case that proves it: Candidatus Thiomargarita magnifica keeps chromosomes inside membrane-bound compartments, so this same test would answer eukaryotic for it, and it is a bacterium. Ancestry settled that, from sequence comparison. The other three descriptions here are distractors of different kinds. Internal protein-shelled compartments are not a nucleus and do not bear on a criterion about the DNA specifically; carboxysomes are exactly such a compartment and occur in bacteria. A 40-hour generation time is a tendency running the wrong way, and Mycobacterium tuberculosis already breaks that tendency at 18 to 24 hours. The 3 micrometre width is likewise a tendency, and a bacterium 2 centimetres long is on record. Weighing four facts and taking a majority verdict is the habit this item is testing for.
commonErrors: Choosing eukaryotic because the cell has internal compartments: the criterion is about one compartment, around one thing, and prokaryotes build others.
Choosing eukaryotic because the organism divides slowly: division rate is a tendency with documented exceptions and never decides classification.
Choosing undecidable: only one of the four descriptions is definitional, so the other three cannot outvote it.
Treating the criterion's answer as the organism's group membership rather than as what the criterion supports, which is the error the giant bacterium exists to catch.

items.prompt: Select every statement that follows directly from whether a membrane envelope encloses a cell's DNA. Leave unselected anything that is only made possible by that arrangement, anything that is a tendency with exceptions, and anything the criterion does not license at all.

options.text: A ribosome can begin translating a transcript that RNA polymerase is still making.
A transcript made from a gene in the nucleus cannot be read until it has crossed the envelope.
Transcripts are checked for defects and the faulty ones held back before any ribosome reads them.
The cell is less than 10 micrometres across.
The cell has no internal compartments of any kind.
The cell type is the older of the two.

answer.summary: Only the two statements about where transcription and translation sit relative to each other.
answer.reasoning: Both correct options are consequences of the same structural fact: if a membrane stands between the nuclear DNA and the ribosomes, transcription and translation of those genes are in different places and a transcript must cross before it is read; if no membrane stands between them, a ribosome can reach a transcript as it is made. Checking transcripts and holding back the faulty ones is the tier this item was rebuilt to test. The separation makes it possible, and nothing more: a membrane does not inspect anything, and the processing, quality control and selective export that follow all need machinery the envelope does not supply. Collapsing made possible into follows directly is the error the lesson exists to prevent, and it is easiest to make on the option that sounds most like the point of a nucleus. Size is a tendency, and a bacterium 2 centimetres long exists. The claim that prokaryotic cells have no internal compartments is simply false, because bacteria build carboxysomes, magnetosomes and other organelles. Which cell type is older is a question about ancestry, settled by sequence comparison rather than by architecture, and eukaryotes emerge from within the Archaea rather than after prokaryotes as a whole.
acceptableResponses: option-follows-coupled and option-follows-processing selected, with no others
commonErrors: Selecting the quality-control statement: the separation makes it possible, and a membrane by itself checks nothing. This is the discriminating option.
Selecting the size statement: it is the tendency tier, and the lesson supplies a counterexample four orders of magnitude away.
Selecting the no-compartments statement: it feels like it should follow from a criterion about a compartment, but the criterion concerns one compartment around one thing.
Selecting the age statement: architecture does not establish ancestry, and the phylogenomic evidence points the other way.

items.prompt: An archaeal cell is modelled as a sphere 1.5 micrometres across. Using the relation for a sphere, give its surface area per unit volume in reciprocal micrometres, to two significant figures.

answer.reasoning: For a sphere, surface area per unit volume is three divided by the radius. The cell is 1.5 micrometres across, so its radius is 0.75 micrometres, and 3 divided by 0.75 gives 4.0 per micrometre. Comparing with the values from the worked example: this cell sits between the modelled bacterium at about 5.0 and the modelled human cell at 0.30, closer to the bacterium, as its size suggests.
commonErrors: Answering 2.0 by dividing three by the diameter instead of the radius; the relation is three over r, and r is half of what was stated.
Answering 8.0 by inverting the division; check that a smaller cell gives a larger ratio, not a smaller one.
Omitting units: the answer is a reciprocal length, and its units are part of the result.

items.prompt: Using the relation between diffusion time and distance, with a diffusion coefficient of 7.7 square micrometres per second, what is the characteristic time over which a protein diffuses a distance of 15 micrometres, the width of a cell? Give your answer to two significant figures. This is the time at which typical displacement reaches that distance, not a delivery time for any particular molecule.

answer.summary: About 15 seconds, as a characteristic timescale rather than an arrival time.
answer.reasoning: The relation is time equals distance squared divided by twice the diffusion coefficient. Fifteen squared is 225, and twice 7.7 is 15.4, so the time is 225 divided by 15.4, which is 14.6 seconds. Sanity-check it against the worked example: a 20 micrometre cell gave 26 seconds, and 15 micrometres is three-quarters of 20, so the answer should be about nine sixteenths of 26, which is 14.6. That agreement is the square law showing up again. What the number is worth is worth stating. It is the time at which root-mean-square displacement equals 15 micrometres, which is a characteristic scale and not a schedule. Diffusion has no arrival time: some molecules cross far sooner, some much later, and turning this into a latency would need a starting position, a geometry and boundary conditions that the question does not give. Read it as an order of magnitude, which is all the source supports and all the lesson's argument needs.
acceptableResponses: Any answer between 13 and 16 seconds, since the relation supports an order of magnitude rather than two-figure precision.
commonErrors: Answering 0.97 by forgetting to square the distance; the square is the entire point of the relation.
Answering 29.2 by dividing by the diffusion coefficient rather than by twice it.
Answering 19.5 by using the 20 micrometre worked value scaled linearly instead of by the square of the ratio.
Reading the result as the time at which a newly made protein arrives at the far end, which treats a characteristic scale as a delivery schedule.

items.prompt: Two spherical cells differ by a factor of 10 in radius. Explain, in your own words and without doing any arithmetic beyond stating factors, why one consequence of that difference is a factor of 10 and the other is a factor of 100. Name which is which and say what each one constrains for the cell.

answer.correct: Surface area per unit volume goes as three over the radius, so a tenfold larger radius gives a tenth of the ratio, a factor of 10. Diffusion time goes as the square of the distance, so a tenfold larger cell takes a hundred times as long to cross, a factor of 100. The first constrains supply, because everything the cell takes in or gives out has to cross its surface and each unit of interior now has a tenth as much membrane serving it. The second constrains coordination, because anything moving by diffusion alone takes a hundred times longer to get anywhere, so a large cell cannot rely on parts finding each other and needs directed transport and local organisation instead.
answer.summary: Surface per unit volume falls as 1/r, giving 10; diffusion time rises as the square of distance, giving 100. The first constrains supply, the second coordination.
answer.reasoning: The two relations carry different powers of the size, and that is the whole reason the answers differ. Surface-to-volume is three over the radius, an inverse first power, so ten times the radius gives one tenth the ratio. Diffusion time is distance squared over twice the diffusion coefficient, a second power, so ten times the distance gives a hundred times the time. Growing a cell therefore hurts its internal mixing far more than it hurts its supply, which is why a large cell needs internal organisation rather than merely more membrane.
acceptableResponses: Any answer that identifies the inverse first power for surface-to-volume and the second power for diffusion time, assigns the factors of 10 and 100 correctly, and states that the first bears on exchange or supply across the surface and the second on internal transport, mixing, coordination, or signalling.
commonErrors: Giving both consequences the same factor: this is the single most common error and it comes from not reading the exponents.

Assigning the factor of 100 to the surface ratio, usually by remembering that area goes as the square of a length and stopping there; the ratio in question divides area by volume, and volume goes as the cube.
Describing the consequences without saying what each constrains, which answers half the question.

items.prompt: A classmate asks why a cell would bother enclosing its DNA at all, since the envelope only seems to get in the way. Answer in a short paragraph. State what the envelope makes possible, state what it costs, and give one reason a colonic lining cell can afford that cost while a bacterium in the lumen might not.

answer.correct: The envelope separates transcription from translation, so a transcript cannot be read the moment it is made. It has to be finished, modified, have non-coding stretches removed, pass quality control, and be exported before a ribosome sees it. Every one of those steps is a place the cell can decide something, so the compartment converts a one-step process into a staged one with control points a shared compartment cannot have. What it costs is transport and time: transcripts out, proteins in, through pores, with machinery to recognise what is allowed through. A bacterium can have new protein appearing while a gene is still being read, and a eukaryotic cell cannot. A colonic lining cell can afford the delay because its job is to hold a barrier for a few days and then be replaced, so it is not competing on speed of response; a bacterium in the lumen is competing for nutrients and space against everything else there, where responding quickly is worth more than regulating finely.
answer.summary: The envelope buys staged regulation of gene expression and charges transport and time; the lining cell's job tolerates the delay, while a lumen bacterium is competing on speed.
answer.reasoning: A complete answer has three parts and they are graded separately. The benefit must be about regulation made possible by separating transcription from translation, not merely protecting the DNA. The cost must name transport, machinery, or delay, and ideally the loss of coupled transcription and translation. The third part asks the learner to relate the trade-off to what each cell actually has to do, which is the transfer step: the lining cell holds a barrier on a several-day schedule and is replaced, while a lumen bacterium competes in a crowded environment where a fast response matters. Answers that say the nucleus protects DNA from damage are outside what this lesson established and should be marked as unsupported rather than wrong.
acceptableResponses: Any answer that names staged regulation, processing, or quality control before translation as the benefit; names transport, machinery, or delay as the cost; and gives a defensible reason connected to what each cell has to do rather than to a ranking of the two cell types.
commonErrors: Saying the nucleus exists to protect the DNA: this may be true in other treatments but is not what this lesson established, and it does not explain the regulatory consequence.
Naming a benefit but no cost, which misses half of what a trade-off means.
Justifying the third part by calling eukaryotic cells more advanced, which is the ranking error the lesson repairs.

items.prompt: Escherichia coli in rich broth doubles in under 20 minutes; a human cell in culture takes about 24 hours; Mycobacterium tuberculosis, which is prokaryotic, also takes about 24 hours. Account for all three figures. Your answer must make clear which parts of the difference the architectural criterion explains and which parts it does not.

answer.correct: Most of the gap between the first two figures is about how much work a division is. A human cell copies roughly six billion base pairs, because a diploid cell holds two copies of a genome of about three billion, spread over 46 chromosome copies, and then has to sort them so each daughter gets a full set. In human cells that sorting uses chromosome condensation, a spindle, and taking the nuclear envelope apart and rebuilding it. A bacterium copies a few million base pairs on one circular molecule. Be careful about what that buys as an explanation. Having the DNA enclosed does not by itself entail a large genome, many linear chromosomes, or that particular way of dividing: bacteria organise and segregate their chromosomes too, and eukaryotic lineages differ in how their mitosis is arranged. The honest statement is that these things travel together in the two cells being compared, and that the amount to be copied and the sorting machinery are what the time is spent on, not that the criterion produces them. The third figure shows the limit plainly. Mycobacterium tuberculosis has the bacterial architecture and none of that extra work, and it is still as slow as a human cell, so architecture cannot be what sets the rate. Division rate belongs on the tendency branch of the model, and its causes in any particular organism lie in its own metabolism and cell envelope rather than in whether its DNA is enclosed.
answer.summary: The work of a division — about six billion base pairs copied across 46 chromosome copies in a diploid human cell, plus the sorting machinery — accounts for the first gap; those features travel with the architecture rather than being entailed by it; and the mycobacterium shows that architecture does not set the rate, so division time is a tendency.
answer.reasoning: The item tests whether the learner can use the model and also say where it stops. The first half should connect the human figure to the amount of DNA and to the sorting machinery a large, enclosed, multi-chromosome genome requires, and should use a per-cell figure: a diploid human cell copies about six billion base pairs, not the three billion of a single haploid assembly. An answer quoting three billion as the amount a human cell copies has halved the work and does not earn that part. Claiming that nuclear enclosure entails genome size, linear chromosomes or open mitosis also does not earn it, because none of those follows from the criterion. The second half is the discriminating part: a prokaryotic organism dividing as slowly as a human cell shows that the criterion does not determine rate, so the learner must relocate the claim from the consequence tier to the tendency tier. An answer that explains the first two figures well and treats the third as an anomaly has not met the second requirement.
acceptableResponses: Any answer that connects the human figure to the per-cell amount of DNA and to the machinery required to sort many enclosed chromosomes, treats those as travelling with the architecture rather than as entailed by it, and uses the mycobacterium to conclude that division rate is a tendency rather than something the criterion determines.
Quoting about 6.1 billion, or two copies of about 3.05 billion, or roughly 6 billion base pairs are all acceptable for the diploid figure.
commonErrors: Quoting three billion base pairs as the amount a human cell copies, which is one haploid assembly rather than what a diploid cell replicates.
Saying that enclosing the DNA is why the genome is large or why there are many linear chromosomes, which the criterion does not entail.
Explaining the first two figures and calling the mycobacterium an exception without drawing the conclusion, which leaves the tendency and the consequence tiers still confused.
Claiming the mycobacterium must therefore be closer to a eukaryote, which reintroduces the ranking error.
Attributing the whole difference to cell size, which the lesson's own numbers do not support: size affects mixing and supply, and the division work is set by what has to be copied and sorted.

items.prompt: A study group is designing a molecule intended to shut down protein synthesis in bacteria and leave human cells untouched. Using only this lesson's model, name the structural difference the design would exploit, say which tier of the model that difference belongs to and why that matters, and name the one place inside a human cell where the design's assumption breaks down. This is a reasoning exercise about cell architecture and is not a question about treating anyone.

answer.correct: The difference to exploit is between the bacterial ribosome and the eukaryotic cytoplasmic ribosome, which differ enough that a molecule can bind one and not the other; whole drug classes already work this way, and eukaryotic cytoplasmic ribosomes are insensitive to several of them. That difference belongs on the correlate branch rather than the consequence branch, because nothing about a membrane around DNA determines the sequence of a ribosomal RNA. It matters because a correlate carries less weight than a consequence: it holds where it has been checked and cannot be assumed everywhere. The assumption breaks down inside the mitochondria, whose ribosomes retain bacterial-like features and are susceptible to drugs the cytoplasmic ribosomes ignore; one 2001 study's authors proposed that susceptibility as the source of the in-vivo toxicity of some such drugs, with aminoglycoside ear and kidney toxicity as their example. Hold that at the strength it was offered: it is one proposed mechanism among several, and both the susceptibility and the route to toxicity vary by drug and by tissue. What the lesson needs from it is that a eukaryotic cell contains a compartment where the assumption fails, not a settled account of why any particular drug harms anyone.
answer.summary: Exploit the ribosome difference; it sits on the correlate branch, not the consequence branch; and it fails inside the mitochondria.
answer.reasoning: This is the transfer item, and it asks for three separate moves. Naming the ribosome is recall. Placing it on the correlate branch is the model being used rather than recited, and the reason must be that architecture does not determine ribosome sequence. Naming the mitochondria is the payoff, and it earns the point on the structural claim alone; an answer is not required to explain clinical toxicity, and one that presents the mitochondrial mechanism as the established cause of it has overstated a medium-confidence proposal and should be marked as overstating rather than as wrong.  a learner who filed the ribosome difference under consequences would predict that anything eukaryotic is safe, and the mitochondrial exception is exactly the prediction failing. Answers may add that the drug will also remove resident gut bacteria, which is correct and is credited, but it does not substitute for naming the mitochondrial exception.
acceptableResponses: Any answer that names the ribosome difference, places it on the correlate or tendency tier with a reason connected to architecture not determining ribosome structure, and identifies the mitochondrial ribosome as where the assumption fails.
commonErrors: Naming the nuclear envelope as the difference to exploit, which confuses the criterion with the structural difference a ribosome-targeting molecule actually acts on.
Filing the ribosome difference under consequences, which produces the over-confident prediction that any eukaryotic cell is safe.
Missing the mitochondrial exception, which is the whole reason the item distinguishes tiers.
Presenting the mitochondrial ribosome as the established reason ribosome-targeting drugs are toxic, which states one proposed mechanism as a settled one.
