claims.statement: A 70 kg reference adult carries about 3.8 x 10^13 bacteria and about 3.0 x 10^13 human cells, so the two populations are of the same order of magnitude, and the colon holds more bacteria than every other body site by at least two orders of magnitude.
claims.scope: Estimates assembled for a 70 kg reference adult male from published densities and organ volumes, not measurements of any individual.
claims.uncertainty: The authors report substantial uncertainty on both figures and revise earlier ratios of 10:1 and 100:1. Only the order-of-magnitude comparison is used in the lesson.

claims.statement: The intestinal epithelium is a single, continuous layer of cells organised into crypts and villi, acting as a semipermeable barrier between the gut microbes and the underlying host immune system.
claims.scope: Human and mammalian intestinal epithelium as described in a 2019 review of epithelial and bacterial interaction.

claims.statement: Cells divide into two structural classes according to whether their DNA is enclosed by a membrane envelope: in a prokaryotic cell the DNA sits in the nucleoid, which unlike the eukaryotic nucleus is not surrounded by a membrane separating it from the cytoplasm, while a eukaryotic cell contains a nucleus and organises its DNA as linear rather than circular molecules.
claims.scope: The standard structural definition of the two cell classes as stated in a cell-biology textbook chapter. It describes cell architecture and is not a statement about evolutionary relatedness.
claims.uncertainty: Organisms exist that sit awkwardly against a criterion stated as a bright line; the lesson presents one of them as a boundary case rather than suppressing it.

claims.statement: A typical prokaryotic cell such as Escherichia coli is surrounded by a rigid cell wall with the plasma membrane inside it, holds its DNA as a single circular molecule in the nucleoid, and contains approximately 30,000 ribosomes distributed through the cytoplasm.
claims.scope: Escherichia coli as the stated exemplar of prokaryotic cell structure. Capsules, plasmids, pili and flagella are present in many but not all bacteria and are labelled in the figure rather than asserted as universal.

claims.statement: The majority of animal cells are 10 to 20 micrometres in diameter and rarely vary more than two-fold outside that band.
claims.scope: Animal cells generally. The 20 micrometre figure used in this lesson's geometry is a working value taken from the top of that band, not a measurement of a colonic cell.
claims.uncertainty: Cell sizes across the human body span many orders of magnitude, so a single working figure is a modelling choice rather than a constant.

claims.statement: Much of the colonic epithelium is renewed on a three-to-five-day timescale, with absorptive cells replaced every four to five days.
claims.scope: Human colonic epithelium under normal conditions. The interval describes population-level turnover and does not assert that every crypt cell shares one lifetime.
claims.uncertainty: Reported intervals vary between studies and between cell types; the lesson uses four days as a round working figure inside the reported range.

claims.statement: Escherichia coli is rod-shaped, about 1 micrometre in diameter and about 2 micrometres long, and most bacterial cells have diameters of 1 to 10 micrometres.
claims.scope: Escherichia coli as a stated textbook exemplar. Bacterial dimensions vary with species and with growth condition.
claims.uncertainty: An independent measurement across 22 growth conditions gives a condition-independent diameter of 1.26 plus or minus 0.16 micrometres, wider than the 1 micrometre figure used in the lesson's model; the lesson records the disagreement and treats its modelled volume as a lower bound.

claims.statement: Measured across 22 growth conditions, single Escherichia coli cells span 1.5 to 4.4 femtolitres in volume, with lengths from 1.6 to 3.9 micrometres and a condition-independent diameter of 1.26 plus or minus 0.16 micrometres.
claims.scope: Laboratory cultures of Escherichia coli across 22 defined growth conditions. One femtolitre equals one cubic micrometre.

claims.statement: Eukaryotic cells are generally much larger than prokaryotic cells, frequently having a cell volume at least a thousandfold greater.
claims.scope: A general comparison between the two cell classes, stated as a floor rather than a typical value.
claims.uncertainty: The comparison is a generalisation with documented exceptions at both ends; the lesson names a centimetre-long bacterium as one of them.

claims.statement: Modelling Escherichia coli as a cylinder 2 micrometres long and 1 micrometre across and a human cell as a sphere 20 micrometres across gives volumes of about 1.6 and 4.2 x 10^3 cubic micrometres, surface areas of about 7.9 and 1.3 x 10^3 square micrometres, and surface-to-volume ratios of about 5.0 and 0.30 per micrometre, so the modelled human cell holds roughly 2.7 x 10^3 times the volume with about one seventeenth of the surface per unit volume.
claims.scope: Arithmetic performed by this lesson on the sourced cell dimensions, using a cylinder and a sphere as declared idealisations of a rod-shaped bacterium and an animal cell.
claims.uncertainty: The result depends on the geometric idealisation and on which value inside the stated size bands is chosen. The modelled bacterial volume of 1.6 cubic micrometres sits at the bottom of the independently measured 1.5 to 4.4 femtolitre range, and the modelled volume ratio sits above the independently stated thousandfold floor.

claims.statement: The apparent diffusion coefficient of green fluorescent protein in the cytoplasm of living Escherichia coli is 7.7 plus or minus 2.5 square micrometres per second, about eleven-fold lower than in water, and a small protein is expected to diffuse across about 1 micrometre in of order 100 milliseconds.
claims.scope: One fluorescent protein measured in one Escherichia coli strain. Larger proteins in the same study diffused several times more slowly.
claims.uncertainty: The stated uncertainty is about a third of the value. Applying this coefficient to a human cell is a declared idealisation used to isolate the effect of geometry.

claims.statement: In the cytoplasm of cultured mammalian cells expressing green fluorescent protein, the measured diffusion coefficient is about 26 plus or minus 3 square micrometres per second, higher than the value measured in Escherichia coli.
claims.scope: Six measurements in one cultured cell line by one method. Reported values for protein mobility in mammalian cytoplasm vary with cell type, probe and technique.
claims.uncertainty: This measurement and the bacterial one were made by different groups using different methods, so the comparison is indicative rather than controlled. It is used only to show that the lesson's conclusion survives replacing the idealised common coefficient with cell-specific values.

claims.statement: In bacteria, transcription and translation occur in the same compartment and a ribosome can begin translating a nascent messenger RNA that RNA polymerase is still transcribing, whereas in eukaryotes a nuclear envelope separates the two processes; tight coupling is not universal across prokaryotes or across growth conditions.
claims.scope: Bacterial and eukaryotic gene expression as described in two reviews published in 2023 and 2024. The qualification about variability comes from the 2024 review.
claims.uncertainty: The degree of physical coupling between polymerase and ribosome, and how general it is across species and conditions, remains an active research question.

claims.statement: Confining transcription to the nucleus adds a layer of regulatory potential that a shared compartment cannot offer, because a transcript can be processed and pass quality control before it is exported and translated in the cytoplasm.
claims.scope: Eukaryotic gene expression as described in a 2024 review of co-transcriptional gene regulation.
claims.uncertainty: The lesson presents this as what the compartment makes possible, not as a claim that every eukaryotic transcript is regulated at every one of these steps.

claims.statement: Bacterial DNA contents range from about 0.6 million to 5 million base pairs, with Escherichia coli K-12 carrying a single circular chromosome of 4.639 million base pairs, while the first gapless human genome assembly totals 3,054,815,472 base pairs of nuclear DNA across 22 autosomes and chromosome X.
claims.scope: Bacteria generally, one Escherichia coli laboratory strain, and one completely assembled human genome. The human figure is a single assembly rather than an average across people.
claims.uncertainty: Genome sizes vary between strains and individuals; the lesson uses only the order-of-magnitude ratio of roughly a thousand.

claims.statement: Escherichia coli doubling times measured at 37 degrees Celsius by three independent methods were 17 to 18 minutes in Luria-Bertani broth and 51 to 54 minutes in a defined minimal medium.
claims.scope: Laboratory culture at a stated temperature in two stated media. These are maxima achievable under favourable conditions and do not describe growth in a human gut.
claims.uncertainty: Doubling times vary with strain, medium, temperature and starting concentration; the lesson uses the rich-medium figure explicitly as an upper bound.

claims.statement: A typical eukaryotic cell cycle is illustrated by human cells in culture, which divide approximately every 24 hours, with mitosis and cytokinesis lasting about an hour so that approximately 95 per cent of the cycle is spent in interphase.
claims.scope: Rapidly proliferating human cells in culture. Cycle times differ widely between cell types and between cells in culture and cells in tissue.
claims.uncertainty: The lesson uses this as a representative figure for a dividing human cell and does not claim it as the cycle time of any colonic cell.

claims.statement: Intestinal stem cells divide about once every 24 hours, and the intestinal epithelium is replaced with a turnover time of three to five days under normal conditions.
claims.scope: Intestinal stem cells under normal conditions as described in a 2021 review of the crypt niche; much of the underlying work is in mouse models.
claims.uncertainty: Division rates are heterogeneous within the stem-cell population and change under injury or inflammation.

claims.statement: Molecular sequence data support a primary division of the living world into three domains, Archaea, Bacteria and Eucarya, and neither the five-kingdom taxonomy nor the eukaryote-prokaryote dichotomy reflects that primary division.
claims.scope: The 1990 proposal that introduced the domain rank and the names Archaea, Bacteria and Eucarya.
claims.uncertainty: Whether Eucarya is best treated as a third primary domain or as a lineage arising within Archaea is itself an active question, and the lesson presents the later two-domain evidence alongside this proposal.

claims.statement: Phylogenomic analyses across independent datasets place eukaryotes as emerging from within archaeal diversity, with the Asgard archaea as the prokaryotic lineages most closely related to eukaryotes.
claims.scope: A 2018 phylogenomic analysis written as a defence of the two-domain topology against a competing interpretation.
claims.uncertainty: The topology of the tree near the origin of eukaryotes is an active area of dispute; the lesson states this and uses the result only to show that a group defined by an absence need not be a single branch.

claims.statement: Prokaryotic cells build internal organelles, including the membrane-bound anammoxosome, magnetosome, chromatophore and chlorosome, and protein-shelled bacterial microcompartments such as the carboxysome, which encloses Rubisco and carbonic anhydrase behind a selectively permeable protein shell.
claims.scope: Bacteria as described in a 2021 review of the carboxysome. These structures occur in particular lineages rather than in every bacterium.

claims.statement: Candidatus Thiomargarita magnifica reaches a maximal cell size of about 2 centimetres in length and 50 micrometres in diameter, carries very large numbers of genome copies, and holds one or more chromosomes inside membrane-bound organelles called pepins.
claims.scope: One described giant sulphur-oxidising bacterium, reported in a 2023 review that cites the 2022 primary description. It is an extreme outlier and not a typical bacterium.
claims.uncertainty: The primary description is recent and the organism has not been cultured; the lesson uses it only as a counterexample to two stated tendencies and as a boundary case for the architectural criterion.

claims.statement: Mycobacterium tuberculosis multiplies very slowly on enriched media, with doubling times of 18 to 24 hours.
claims.scope: In-vitro growth on enriched laboratory media, as stated in a medical microbiology textbook chapter.
claims.uncertainty: The chapter dates from 1996; the doubling-time figure is a stable and widely repeated one, but the lesson pairs its culture-time figures with a current source.

claims.statement: On solid media inoculated with clinical material, identifiable mycobacterial colonies may not appear for four to six weeks, while broth systems require only 5 to 12 days; the 2014 study cited reports that at the time of writing a primary culture was obtained in two to four weeks on average and phenotypic antibiotic susceptibility after a further two to four weeks. These are culture timings from that study and not a current description of tuberculosis diagnosis, which now leads with rapid molecular testing; how much an interim negative means depends on the specimen, the bacterial burden, the culture system and protocol, and whether the result in hand is molecular or culture-based.
claims.scope: Diagnostic mycobacterial culture. The solid-media and broth figures come from a 1996 textbook chapter and the current-practice figures from a 2014 study.
claims.uncertainty: Turnaround times depend on the laboratory, the system used, and the bacterial load in the specimen, and have shortened since the older figures were written. The lesson uses these as an independent check on an order-of-magnitude estimate rather than as operational guidance.

claims.statement: Eukaryotic cytoplasmic ribosomes are insensitive to macrolides, lincosamides, streptomycin and 2-deoxystreptamines while bacterial ribosomes are sensitive to them, and the selectivity of a drug affecting protein synthesis is often determined by a single nucleotide or amino acid.
claims.scope: Ribosome-targeting antibacterial drug classes as analysed in a 2001 study of resistance mutations and comparative sequence. Educational use only; no drug is named as a treatment for any condition.
claims.uncertainty: Susceptibility patterns vary by organism and by drug within each class, and resistance changes them; the lesson uses the statement only to show that architectural difference can be exploited pharmacologically.

claims.statement: Mitochondrial ribosomes retain bacterial-like features, and the authors of a 2001 study propose that the in-vivo toxicity of some ribosome-targeting drugs follows from susceptibility of the mitochondrial ribosome, with aminoglycoside ototoxicity and nephrotoxicity as their standing example. It is one proposed mechanism among several, and both susceptibility and the mechanism of toxicity vary by agent and by tissue.
claims.scope: An interpretation offered by the authors of that study, presented in the lesson as their proposal rather than as settled mechanism. Educational use only; nothing here is guidance about any drug or patient.
claims.uncertainty: Aminoglycoside ototoxicity has several proposed contributing mechanisms; the lesson uses this one to show that the two-architecture picture has a documented internal exception.

claims.statement: Perturbation of the gut microbiota by antibiotic administration allows Clostridioides difficile spores to germinate into vegetative forms that colonise the intestine and produce toxins; TcdA and TcdB inactivate proteins of the Rho family, altering cellular integrity and morphology, causing loss of tight junctions and increased permeability of the intestinal epithelial layer, with presentations ranging from mild diarrhoea to pseudomembranous colitis and toxic megacolon.
claims.scope: Mechanism of Clostridioides difficile colonisation and toxin-mediated epithelial damage as described in a 2024 review. Presented as a teaching example; the lesson makes no claim about incidence, risk, prevention, or treatment and gives no clinical guidance.
claims.uncertainty: The frequency of infection after antibiotic exposure depends heavily on agent, duration, setting and host factors, none of which the lesson asserts.

claims.statement: The colon carries a microbial load of about 10^11 bacteria per millilitre of content.
claims.scope: Human colonic contents, stated as an order-of-magnitude density in a 2019 review.
claims.uncertainty: Densities vary along the gut and between individuals; only the order of magnitude is used.

terms.definition: A cell whose DNA is not enclosed by a membrane envelope of its own but lies in the cytoplasm, in a dense region called the nucleoid. Bacteria and archaea are prokaryotic. The term names one architectural feature and carries no implication about age, complexity, size, or division rate, despite an etymology meaning before the kernel. The word covers both bacteria and archaea, which are not each other's closest relatives, so it names a way of being built rather than one group of relatives. At least one bacterium keeps its chromosomes inside membrane-bound compartments and is a bacterium regardless, because ancestry decides that and architecture does not.

A cell whose DNA is enclosed by a membrane envelope of its own, forming a nucleus. Animals, plants, fungi and protists are built from eukaryotic cells, including the colonic lining cells this module follows. Membership in the group is decided by ancestry rather than by this description of how the cell is built, so the envelope is how the word gets applied and not what the word means.

The membrane-bounded compartment of a eukaryotic cell that contains its DNA, together with the envelope that encloses it. Everyday English uses nucleus to mean the middle or the core of something; here it means this specific compartment, and a cell can have a middle without having one.
The region of a prokaryotic cell where the DNA is concentrated. It is not separated from the rest of the cytoplasm by a membrane, which is the single feature that distinguishes it from a nucleus.

The interior of a cell outside its nucleus, including the fluid and everything suspended or embedded in it. In a prokaryotic cell the cytoplasm is one continuous space holding the DNA and the ribosomes together.

The machine that builds a protein by reading a messenger RNA transcript. Bacterial ribosomes and eukaryotic cytoplasmic ribosomes differ enough in structure that a drug can bind one and not the other, which is why some antibacterial drugs leave host cells running.

A small DNA loop separate from a bacterium's main chromosome, which the cell can gain, lose, or pass to a neighbour. Plasmid transfer is one route by which antibiotic resistance spreads between bacteria.

The complete DNA sequence a cell carries, measured in base pairs. A bacterial genome is usually a single circular molecule of a few million base pairs; the human nuclear genome is about three billion base pairs across more than twenty linear chromosomes.

Separating activities of a cell into different enclosed spaces so that each can be run and regulated on its own terms. In this lesson the compartment in question is the nucleus, and what it buys is the chance to process and check a transcript before any ribosome reads it.

The surface area a body has per unit of its volume, written A/V and carried in reciprocal micrometres for cells. For a sphere of radius r it equals 3/r, so it falls as a cell grows. It decides how much membrane is available to serve each unit of interior.

The spreading of molecules by random thermal motion, with no motor or flow pushing them. The average of the squared distance covered grows in proportion to time, so the time to cross a distance grows as the square of that distance: ten times further costs a hundred times longer.

The time a cell population takes to double in number under stated conditions. It is a property of an organism and its circumstances together, not of the organism alone: Escherichia coli doubles in about 18 minutes in rich broth and about 52 minutes in a minimal medium.

In classification, the highest rank above kingdom. Cellular life is divided into three: Bacteria, Archaea and Eucarya. This is a taxonomic sense of the word and is unrelated to the set of inputs on which a function is defined.

alignment.note: PREM-QNT-005 and PREM-QNT-007 use domain for the set of inputs on which an expression or a function is defined. Biology uses the same word for the highest rank in classification, above kingdom. The two senses are unconnected, and the lesson says so in prose at the point where the taxonomic sense first appears, so a learner who already holds the mathematical meaning is not left reconciling them.

terms.definition: One of the three domains of cellular life. Archaeal cells are prokaryotic, in that no membrane envelope encloses their DNA, and phylogenomic evidence places eukaryotes as arising from within this group rather than alongside it.

Original contribution

The lesson prose, the cylinder-and-sphere geometry and every factor derived from it, the crossing-time comparison, the criterion diagram and its three tiers, the surface-to-volume chart, the generations-per-renewal arithmetic, the twenty-seven-doublings estimate and its check against published culture times, the constructed deep-sea organism, the constructed engineered bacterium, the constructed gut organism, all tables, prompts, feedback, assessment items, rubrics, and glossary definitions were created for EmbeddedKnowledge and are contributed under CC BY 4.0 by the accountable principal.

Three visuals appear in this pack: one third-party figure and two original artefacts.

  • assets/prokaryote-cell-labelled.png is third party. It is Average prokaryote cell by Mariana Ruiz Villarreal (LadyofHats), released by its author into the public domain, from the file page for File:Average prokaryote cell- en.svg on Wikimedia Commons. The licence was verified on the file's own Commons page rather than on any front page, search result, or mirror. The page's structured data records copyright status as copyrighted, dedicated to the public domain by copyright holder and copyright licence as released into the public domain by the copyright holder. A fully labelled animal-cell diagram teaches the organelle inventory, which is lesson 03's outcome rather than this one's, and at the 20vh cap the guided reader applies to a figure its twenty labels would not be legible. Terminology continuity

The course terminology ledger was read before the glossary was designed. Thirteen of the fourteen entries introduce terms no published lesson currently owns: prokaryotic cell, eukaryotic cell, cell nucleus, nucleoid, cytoplasm, ribosome, plasmid, genome, compartmentalisation, surface-to-volume ratio, diffusion, generation time, and archaea. One declares an alignment block in glossary.json.

  • domain — distinct-sense against PREM-QNT-007. PREM-QNT-005 and PREM-QNT-007 both use domain for the set of inputs on which an expression or function is defined. Biology uses the same word for the highest rank in classification, above kingdom, which is how it appears in the three-domain proposal this lesson cites. The two senses share nothing but the spelling, so the fourth scene names the collision in prose at the point where the taxonomic sense first appears and links back to the lesson that owns the mathematical sense.

Terms this lesson uses but does not redefine, because PREM-BIO-001 already owns them, are cell, tissue, epithelium, lumen, colonic crypt, stem cell, micrometre, and order of magnitude. Their meanings are carried forward unchanged.

Source use and rights

Twenty-three sources support the factual claims. Adjudication repairs to the 0.1.0 candidate

The academic review returned request-changes with one blocking finding, three major, three minor and one verification note; the learning-design review approved with five notes. All seven actionable findings were repaired in one finalization pass and none was declined.

The blocking finding was right, and it was the lesson arguing with itself. Scene 4 already taught the correct position: a criterion stated as a bright line met an organism sitting on the line, and what settled the organism was ancestry rather than counting membranes. The objective, the scene 1 definition, the diagram, the glossary and four answer keys had never caught up with it. They asked the learner to classify any cell from DNA location alone, which is the exact habit scene 4 spends a page dismantling, and which has no answer for a bacterium whose chromosomes sit inside pepins.

The repair does not weaken the test, because the test is the right place for a learner to start. It states its standing. It is the working criterion, it is how the two words get applied to almost every cell you will meet, and it describes construction rather than deciding membership. The objective now requires the learner to say what the test does not settle. The glossary entries for both cell types say that ancestry decides the group. The diagram gained a branch off the test itself for what the test does not settle at all.

Two consequences of that finding needed separate work. The claim that transcription and translation are separated is true of nuclear genes and not of mitochondrial ones, which are transcribed and translated in the same compartment inside a eukaryotic cell; scene 3, the diagram and the sort item now say so. And the lesson had three tiers where it needed four. Transcript processing and quality control are made possible by the separation, not caused by it — a membrane inspects nothing, and each step needs machinery the envelope does not supply. Scene 3 now names that tier where it first earns it, scene 4's sorting rule has four entries, the diagram has a made-possible branch, and the sort item's discriminating option tests it.

The three majors were all in answer keys.

  • A tier error inside the item that teaches tiers. The sort item's key scored transcript processing and quality control as following directly. The lesson's own claim-nucleus-regulatory-layer scopes them as regulatory potential. The option now states the direct consequence, that a nuclear transcript cannot be read until it has crossed, and a new option carries the quality-control claim as the option a learner should leave unselected.
  • False precision on a diffusion time. Inverting the mean-squared-displacement relation gives the characteristic time at which typical displacement reaches a distance, not the latency for a protein to cross a cell. The cited source supports an order of magnitude. The prompt now says characteristic time and says what it is not, the tolerance is loosened from 0.8 to 1.5 seconds, and the key states that diffusion has no arrival time.
  • A ploidy error and an unsupported causal chain. The key used 3,054,815,472 base pairs, one haploid telomere-to-telomere assembly, as the amount a human cell copies. A diploid cell copies roughly six billion across 46 chromosome copies, so the key had halved the work it was asking the learner to explain. It also attributed genome size, linear chromosomes, open mitosis and cycle duration to the nuclear envelope, none of which the criterion entails — bacteria organise and segregate chromosomes too, and eukaryotic lineages differ in mitotic architecture. The key now says these features travel together in the two cells being compared rather than being produced by the criterion, which is the same tier discipline the rest of the lesson teaches, applied to itself.

The three minors: scene 1 asserted functions for the capsule, plasmids, pili and the flagellum that no claim in this pack establishes, so those are now labels with the gap stated; the mycobacterial culture claim called a 2014 study "current tools" and said a two-week negative means almost nothing, and now says what that study reported, that molecular testing leads initial diagnosis while culture stays slow, and that how weak an interim negative is depends on specimen, burden and system; and the mitochondrial ribosome key presented one medium-confidence 2001 proposal as the reason such drugs are toxic at all, and now carries it at the strength it was offered.
